items.good: The reader finds each part under the heading READMEs commonly give it, in the template's order: the opening under the name with no heading, then Example, Why organize-downloads, Requirements, Installation, Documentation, Development and License; each section opens with its main point, and each list item is one sentence, not bold, with its explanation after a blank line and indented under it.

From the opening the reader learns the idea (files sorted into one folder per kind by extension, with a run that only lists the moves, no file ever deleted, renamed or overwritten, and the last move on that folder undoable), the kind of thing that gives it (a command-line tool for macOS and Linux), and whom it is for (anyone whose Downloads folder holds so many files they cannot find the one they want), so they can tell whether it is for them.

The reader sees a Downloads folder like their own before, the listing run's output, the --move run's output and the folder after it, and the --undo run's output and the folder back as at first, with the cases of a taken name, an unknown kind, a hidden file, a download in progress and a folder already there each shown with what happens, so they can picture the three runs on their own folder from starting to the result.

The reader sets the tool against sorting by hand, sorting the view in a file manager and a rule-based organizer, each with the work it leaves them that this tool does (making folders and dragging files, files left together in one folder, rules to write before anything moves), with no benefit every way gives set among them.

parts.good: The opening reads once through: what the tool does, how it chooses (by extension), what it never does and what it can undo, then for whom, each word plain.

Each run is shown as a command block with its output after the folder it runs on; each case is told with what happens in it where it first appears; what the folders already there undergo is said after all three runs have been shown, so it names --move and --undo only once the reader has seen them; running on another folder is a command block to copy; and the extensions of each kind are in a table, with what an extension is said before it.
Each other way is named with an example of it where the name may be unclear (Finder, Files) and the work it leaves, and the comparison points back only to the table the reader has already read.

Each requirement says what it is and why it is needed, and each command the reader runs to check or get it (python3 --version, sudo apt install curl, echo "$PATH", the PATH line) is in a block to copy, with what it prints and what to look for said before it.

The install commands are in one block to copy in the order they run, --help in a block of its own, then the first use points back to the Example the reader has read and tells the macOS access request where they meet it.
Each item says what the page holds and links to it, understood without following the link.
One sentence says what the linked page holds for those who build the tool.
The license is named and its full text linked in one line.

The reader who follows the License link reads the terms once from the top: the name "MIT License" first, then who holds the copyright and from when, then what anyone may do with the software, the one condition of keeping the notice, and the disclaimer of warranty and liability, in the standard MIT wording, each sentence resting only on what came before it ("the Software" defined in the first sentence that uses it).

items.good: Each sentence gives the reader one thing no other gives: the opening says the gain once and Why names only the work other ways leave; what folders already there undergo is said once, after the runs; Installation points to the Example's runs rather than repeating them; the kinds are listed once, in the table; no part speaks to a reviewer, tells the history of a decision, or holds fuller use, which docs/usage.md is for; the license's terms are only in LICENSE, the README naming it and linking there.

questions.question: B-4, B-5 and B-8 of organize-downloads/README.md are found without Good twice by the first user, who uses the README in a newcomer's place, and no change to the README can give them: the download address (README.md line 170) gives 404 and organize-downloads/ holds only README.md and LICENSE, so the reader cannot install the tool, run --help or the Example, or check what the README says the tool does; and the links to docs/usage.md, CHANGELOG.md and docs/architecture.md (lines 187, 189, 193) lead to files not yet there. The CCS already holds your choice that at this design stage these are judged by whether the steps and links give what they say once the build stage has made the tool and those files, but the first user judges them on what the reader gets today, so this run cannot end with them met. Everything else the first user checked holds: the requirements, the macOS access note, every statement set beside AC1-AC12, and LICENSE. How should t1.1 end for these three items?
questions.recommended: End t1.1 with B-4, B-5 and B-8 recorded as to be checked at the build stage, by a first user installing from the address once the tool, docs/usage.md and CHANGELOG.md are on main, and docs/architecture.md once T2 is, because the README already gives all it can at this stage and holding the run open would only repeat the same 404 and missing files until then.

chosen.chosen: LICENSE holds the standard MIT text as the Open Source Initiative gives it, headed "MIT License", with only the decided copyright line filled in.
chosen.why: The decision names the MIT license and its copyright line; the standard text unchanged is what readers and tools recognise as MIT.

chosen.chosen: The download address is https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lovaizu/playground/main/organize-downloads/organize-downloads, the tool's single file named organize-downloads in the organize-downloads folder of main, fetched with curl.
chosen.why: The decision says the file is downloaded into ~/.local/bin; steering.md's pull request is in lovaizu/playground, a raw address on main serves the file as it is, and naming the file as the command means it runs by that name without renaming; curl is on macOS and most Linux systems.

chosen.chosen: Python 3.8 or later is the version the README asks for.
chosen.why: The decision says Python 3 with only its standard library and names no version; 3.8 sets a floor low enough for older systems still in use, which I have not checked against a list of systems, and the tool is to use nothing a later standard library alone gives.

chosen.chosen: The options are --move and --undo, with the folder given after the options and ~/Downloads when none is given, and each line's wording is as the Example shows ("name -> Folder/", "name: stays, <why>", "name: back from Folder/").
chosen.why: steering.md names an option that moves and one that undoes but not their names or the lines' wording; short words that say the action let the reader type them from memory, and the README is what the build and T2 make the tool to.

chosen.chosen: The full list of extensions of each kind is the table in the Example: the steering.md examples plus jpeg, heif, bmp, tif, tiff; doc, xls, ppt, odt, ods, odp, rtf, pages, numbers, key; tgz, bz2, xz; aac, flac, ogg, opus, aiff; avi, webm, m4v, matched in capitals or small letters alike by the part after the last dot.
chosen.why: AC2 leaves the full list to the design and T1 to hold it; these are the common files of each kind met in a Downloads folder on macOS and Linux, and matching the last dot gives archive.tar.gz to Archives with one rule.

chosen.chosen: The PATH line is added to ~/.zshrc on macOS and ~/.bashrc on Linux.
chosen.why: Those are the shells each system starts by default, so a newcomer with no setup of their own finds the line takes effect.

chosen.chosen: The first use tells macOS readers that macOS may ask whether the terminal may access the Downloads folder, and to allow it.
chosen.why: macOS guards the Downloads folder and asks the first time a terminal reads it; a reader who refuses gets no files listed and cannot tell why, and the README says "may" since a terminal already allowed is not asked.
